title: Life Processes – I: Nutrition, Transportation, Respiration and Excretion
summary: ## Nutrition

Life processes are the activities by which organisms take in food, get energy, remove wastes and respond to changes. Food gives energy for life processes, helps growth and repair of tissues, and is needed to make enzymes and hormones. Nutrition is the process of obtaining food, changing it into simple absorbable forms and using it. Autotrophs (green plants, algae, some bacteria) make their own food by photosynthesis — they are the producers of food chains. Heterotrophs depend on others: holozoic nutrition (ingestion, digestion, absorption — Amoeba, frog, humans); parasitic nutrition (head louse, bed bug, worms, leech, the plant Cuscuta); saprotrophic nutrition on dead and decaying matter (mushroom, bread mould, yeast), which cleans the environment.
## Photosynthesis

Green plants make glucose from carbon dioxide and water in the presence of sunlight and chlorophyll, giving out oxygen: 6CO2 + 12H2O → C6H12O6 + 6H2O + 6O2. It is the only process that changes solar energy into chemical energy. Chlorophyll in the chloroplasts of leaf cells traps light; carbon dioxide enters through the stomata, water comes from the roots through the xylem, and oxygen leaves through the stomata. It takes place in a light reaction (light captured) and a dark reaction (glucose formed); glucose is used by cells or stored as starch. Significance: it provides food for all living beings, uses up the carbon dioxide released in respiration and releases the oxygen needed for respiration.
## Nutrients and a balanced diet

Energy-giving nutrients are carbohydrates (sugar, starch, cellulose/roughage — the main energy source) and fats (oil, ghee, butter, nuts; 1 g of fat gives about 37 kJ, i.e. 9 kcal, more than carbohydrates; they keep the body warm). Proteins (milk, pulses, eggs, meat) are body-building. Vitamins and minerals regulate growth. Vitamins: A (milk, carrots) — night blindness; B1 — beri-beri; B12 — anaemia; C (amla, citrus) — scurvy (bleeding gums); D (sunlight, milk) — rickets (soft, deformed bones); E — affects fertility; K (spinach, cabbage) — needed for blood clotting. A, D, E, K are fat-soluble; B and C are water-soluble. Minerals: iron (haemoglobin), calcium (bones, teeth, clotting), potassium, iodine (thyroid, brain development). Water (65–70% of body weight) regulates temperature; raw vegetables give roughage that prevents constipation. A balanced diet contains all nutrients in the right proportion for one's age, sex and work.
## Digestion in humans

The alimentary canal runs mouth → pharynx → oesophagus → stomach → small intestine → large intestine → rectum → anus, with the salivary glands, liver and pancreas. Enzymes, mostly proteins, speed up reactions without being used up. Mouth: salivary amylase changes starch to sugar. Oesophagus: no digestion; food is pushed down by peristalsis. Stomach: gastric juice contains hydrochloric acid (kills bacteria, activates pepsinogen) and pepsin, which breaks proteins into peptones. Small intestine: bile from the liver (stored in the gall bladder) emulsifies fats and makes the medium alkaline; pancreatic juice contains trypsin (proteins), amylase (starch → maltose) and lipase (fats → fatty acids and glycerol); digestion is completed into glucose, amino acids, fatty acids and glycerol. Finger-like villi increase the surface for absorption into the blood. Large intestine absorbs water; faeces leave through the anus. Steps: ingestion, digestion, absorption, assimilation, egestion. Jaundice (yellow skin and urine) is caused by the hepatitis virus infecting the liver.
## Deficiency diseases and adulteration

Malnutrition (inadequate or unbalanced diet) retards growth. Protein-energy malnutrition (PEM): marasmus in infants deprived of mother's milk — wasted muscles, loose folds of skin, prominent ribs, slow growth; kwashiorkor in children of 1–5 years — swelling and enlarged liver due to water retention, dark scaly skin, reddish-brown hair, thin legs, retarded physical and mental growth; cured by a protein-rich diet. Goitre — iodine deficiency, enlarged thyroid (use iodised salt). Anaemia — iron deficiency, less haemoglobin. Food adulteration means mixing cheaper substances into food: stones and husk in cereals, kesari dal and metanil yellow in pulses, water and starch in milk, argemone oil in edible oil, papaya seeds in black pepper.
## Transport in plants

Water and minerals absorbed by root hairs rise through the xylem (non-living tracheids and vessels) to the leaves — the ascent of sap — pulled up by transpiration pull, created when water evaporates from the stomata (transpiration). Food made in the leaves is carried by the living sieve tubes of the phloem to other parts — translocation — and stored in fruits, stems or roots.
## Circulation in humans

The circulatory system has the heart, blood vessels and blood. Arteries carry blood away from the heart (thick, elastic walls); veins bring it back; thin capillaries connect them and allow exchange of materials with tissues. The heart has four chambers — two atria (auricles) above and two ventricles below — made of cardiac muscle that contracts rhythmically without tiring, about 72 times a minute (pulse rate, felt in the radial artery at the wrist); an ECG records its activity. The left ventricle pumps oxygenated blood into the aorta. Arteries carry oxygenated and veins deoxygenated blood, except the pulmonary artery (deoxygenated) and pulmonary vein (oxygenated). Normal blood pressure is 120/80 mm Hg, measured with a sphygmomanometer.

Blood is a connective tissue: plasma with red blood cells (no nucleus, red haemoglobin carries oxygen and carbon dioxide), white blood cells (colourless, fight germs and make antibodies) and platelets (blood clotting); blood cells are made in the bone marrow. It transports nutrients, gases, hormones, wastes and medicines. ABO blood groups: A (gives to A, AB; receives from A, O), B (gives to B, AB; receives from B, O), AB — universal recipient (receives from all, gives only to AB), O — universal donor (gives to all, receives only from O). Mismatched transfusion makes red cells clump (agglutination). Lymph (light yellow) flows one way from tissues to the heart in lymph vessels; its lymphocytes fight infection. Disorders: heart attack (arteries of the heart blocked by fatty deposits), anaemia, leukaemia (blood cancer — too many WBCs), hypertension (high blood pressure — headache, dizziness, fatigue).
## Respiration

Plants have no special respiratory organs: gases are exchanged through stomata in leaves (opened and closed by guard cells that swell when turgid), root hairs, and lenticels in bark. In humans, breathing (exchange of gases with the air) differs from cellular respiration (oxidation of glucose in the mitochondria to release energy as ATP, with carbon dioxide and water). Air passes through the nostrils, nasal cavity, pharynx, glottis, larynx (voice box), trachea (kept open by rings of cartilage), two bronchi and bronchioles to millions of air sacs (alveoli) in the lungs, where oxygen diffuses into capillaries and carbon dioxide diffuses out; alveoli give a huge surface for exchange.

Inhalation: the diaphragm contracts and flattens and the rib muscles raise the ribs up and out; the chest cavity enlarges, pressure falls and air rushes in. Exhalation: the diaphragm relaxes and arches up, ribs move down and in, the chest cavity becomes smaller and air is pushed out. An adult at rest breathes 16–18 times a minute; the rate rises with exercise, fever or stress. Mountaineers and divers carry oxygen; people at high altitudes have more red blood cells.
## Excretion

Excretion is the removal of harmful wastes made in the body. The human excretory (urinary) system has two bean-shaped kidneys, two ureters, the urinary bladder (stores urine) and the urethra. Each kidney has about a million nephrons, its structural and functional units. A nephron has a cup-shaped Bowman's capsule containing a knot of capillaries, the glomerulus, followed by a tubule (proximal convoluted tubule, loop of Henle, distal convoluted tubule). Blood is filtered in the Bowman's capsule (blood cells and proteins stay in the blood); useful substances, water and salts are reabsorbed from the tubule; the remaining waste, mainly urea, forms urine. Kidneys also regulate water content (osmoregulation) and the mineral balance of blood. Skin (sweat), lungs (carbon dioxide) and liver also remove wastes. If both kidneys fail, dialysis (an artificial kidney: blood passes along a membrane bathed in dialysis fluid, which removes wastes, and returns to the body) or a kidney transplant can save the patient.

case.passage: In the human body food is digested step by step. Saliva begins the digestion of starch in the mouth. In the stomach, hydrochloric acid and pepsin act on proteins. In the small intestine, bile from the liver breaks fats into tiny droplets, and pancreatic juice supplies trypsin, amylase and lipase. Digestion is completed here, and the finger-like villi absorb the products into the blood. The large intestine absorbs water from the undigested food.

vsa: Define the terms (i) osmoregulation and (ii) dialysis.

(i) Osmoregulation is the maintenance of the correct amount of water and mineral ions in the blood and body. (ii) Dialysis is the removal of waste from the blood of a person whose kidneys have failed, using an artificial kidney in which blood flows past a membrane bathed in dialysis fluid.
Name two deficiency diseases caused by protein-energy malnutrition. State the symptoms of any one.

Marasmus and kwashiorkor. Marasmus (infants deprived of mother's milk): wasting of muscles, loose folds of skin, prominent ribs, slow growth. (Kwashiorkor: swelling, enlarged liver, dark scaly skin, reddish-brown hair, thin legs, retarded growth.)
Why is hypertension considered a disorder of the circulatory system? Write any two of its symptoms.
Hypertension is high blood pressure — blood pushes too hard against the walls of the arteries, straining the heart and blood vessels. Symptoms: headache, dizziness, fatigue.
Why are we advised to chew our food well?

Chewing breaks food into small pieces and mixes it with saliva, whose amylase starts digesting starch; the moist, small pieces are easy to swallow and give enzymes a larger surface to act on in the stomach and intestine.
Why does the trachea not collapse during exhalation?
The trachea is supported by rings of cartilage, which keep it open even when there is little air in it.
What is the difference between breathing and respiration?

Breathing is the physical process of taking in air and giving out carbon dioxide (exchange of gases in the lungs). Respiration is the oxidation of food (glucose) in the cells to release energy, with production of carbon dioxide and water.
Classify living organisms on the basis of their mode of nutrition.
Autotrophs make their own food by photosynthesis (green plants, algae). Heterotrophs depend on others: holozoic (Amoeba, humans), parasitic (head louse, Cuscuta) and saprotrophic (mushroom, yeast).
sa: A patient's kidneys stop working properly. Explain how dialysis helps in such a situation and why it is important.

In dialysis a tube from an artery takes the patient's blood to an artificial kidney. The blood flows through a tube with a thin membrane surrounded by dialysis fluid; urea and other wastes diffuse out of the blood into the fluid, while blood cells and proteins stay in. The cleaned blood is returned to a vein. It is important because without it nitrogenous wastes and excess water and salts would accumulate in the blood and poison the body; it keeps the patient alive until a kidney transplant.
Describe the processes of transport of water and of food in plants.

Water and minerals absorbed by root hairs move up through the xylem (tracheids and vessels) to the leaves; this ascent of sap is driven by transpiration pull — water evaporating from the stomata pulls the water column up. Food (sugar) made in the leaves is carried by the sieve tubes of the phloem to other parts of the plant (translocation) and stored in roots, stems or fruits.
What is meant by a balanced diet? What are its main constituents? Why should raw vegetables and fruits be regular components of meals?

A balanced diet contains all the essential nutrients in the right amounts and proportion for a person's age, sex and work. Constituents: carbohydrates, fats, proteins, vitamins, minerals, water and roughage. Raw vegetables and fruits supply vitamins and minerals and give roughage (fibre) that helps bowel movement and prevents constipation.
What are enzymes? List three pancreatic enzymes and state their functions.

Enzymes are biological catalysts, mostly proteins, that speed up chemical reactions in the body without being used up. Pancreatic enzymes: trypsin — digests proteins (peptones to peptides); amylase — digests starch into maltose; lipase — digests fats into fatty acids and glycerol.
Explain the mechanism of breathing in humans.

Inhalation: the diaphragm contracts and flattens and the rib muscles lift the ribs up and out; the chest cavity enlarges, the pressure inside falls and air rushes into the lungs. Exhalation: the diaphragm relaxes and arches up, the ribs move down and in; the chest cavity becomes smaller, the pressure rises and air is pushed out through the trachea and nose.
Draw a diagram of the human respiratory system and label the glottis, trachea, lungs and bronchioles.

Diagram: nostrils → nasal cavity → pharynx; the glottis is the opening of the pharynx into the larynx/trachea; the trachea (with cartilage rings) runs down the neck and divides into two bronchi entering the two lungs; inside the lungs the bronchi branch into fine bronchioles ending in alveoli; the diaphragm lies below the lungs.
la: What is photosynthesis? Explain the raw materials required for photosynthesis and how plants obtain them.

Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants make glucose from carbon dioxide and water in the presence of sunlight and chlorophyll, releasing oxygen: 6CO2 + 12H2O → C6H12O6 + 6H2O + 6O2. Raw materials: (1) carbon dioxide — taken from the air through the stomata of leaves; (2) water — absorbed from the soil by root hairs and carried up the xylem to the leaves; (3) sunlight — the source of energy, absorbed by the leaves; (4) chlorophyll — the green pigment in the chloroplasts of leaf cells, which traps light energy. The glucose formed is used or stored as starch and oxygen is released through the stomata.
Explain the digestion of carbohydrates, proteins and fats in human beings.

Carbohydrates: in the mouth salivary amylase converts starch into sugar; in the small intestine pancreatic amylase changes starch to maltose and digestion is completed to glucose. Proteins: in the stomach, hydrochloric acid activates pepsin, which breaks proteins into peptones; in the small intestine trypsin of pancreatic juice breaks them further, and they are finally digested into amino acids. Fats: in the small intestine bile from the liver emulsifies fats into droplets and gives an alkaline medium; lipase of pancreatic juice changes them into fatty acids and glycerol. The end products are absorbed by the villi into the blood.

la: (a) Draw a simple diagram of the human excretory system and label the kidney, ureters, bladder and urethra. (b) Write two important functions of the kidney. (c) What is a nephron?

(a) Two bean-shaped kidneys in the upper abdomen near the back; a ureter from each runs down to the urinary bladder; the urethra leads out from the bladder. (b) Kidneys remove nitrogenous wastes (urea) from the blood as urine, and regulate the water and mineral balance of the body (osmoregulation). (c) A nephron is the structural and functional unit of the kidney — a Bowman's capsule with a glomerulus, where blood is filtered, and a tubule, where useful substances and water are reabsorbed, leaving urine.

(a) Why is a balanced diet essential? Name the nutrients that must be part of it, with an example of each. (b) Deficiency of which nutrient causes anaemia, kwashiorkor and rickets? (c) Which nutrient will not be digested if the pancreas does not secrete lipase?

(a) A balanced diet gives energy, growth, repair and protection against disease. Nutrients: carbohydrates (rice, wheat), fats (ghee, oil), proteins (pulses, milk, eggs), vitamins (fruits, vegetables), minerals (green leafy vegetables, milk), water and roughage (raw vegetables). (b) Anaemia — iron; kwashiorkor — proteins; rickets — vitamin D (and calcium). (c) Fats, since lipase digests fats into fatty acids and glycerol.
